clinicalPearls: Mental or substance use disorders affect roughly 30% of the U.S. population, yet only about one-third of those affected are currently in treatment; four of the ten leading causes of global disability are psychiatric in origin, and depression is the single largest contributor to disability worldwide.

Brief validated office instruments (PRIME-MD / Patient Health Questionnaire, SDDS-PC, the four-item PC-PTSD screen) take only minutes and map patient responses onto formal DSM criteria, helping primary care clinicians make the initial diagnosis.

Panic attacks reach peak intensity within about 10 minutes and usually resolve within an hour; up to ~75% of panic disorder patients eventually meet criteria for major depression, and panic is a frequent occult cause of chest pain with normal coronary angiograms and of unexplained syncope.

Agoraphobia and housebound behavior are often concealed out of embarrassment, so the syndrome is missed unless the clinician asks directly; about one-third of patients presenting with anxiety have an underlying medical etiology.

Major depression requires depressed mood or anhedonia plus a total of at least 5 of 9 symptoms for a minimum of 2 weeks; key distinguishing features from grief are pervasive worthlessness/self-loathing and persistent (rather than wave-like) dysphoria.

Suicide risk must be probed by direct, empathic questioning: about 4-5% of depressed patients die by suicide, and most have seen a physician within the month before death; coexisting anxiety, panic, or agitation raises near-term risk.

Recognizing a bipolar diathesis in a patient presenting with depression is essential because antidepressant monotherapy can worsen symptoms and accelerate cycling; clues include childhood onset, antidepressant treatment failure, atypical features (hypersomnia, weight gain), and marked irritability/impulsivity.

Anorexia nervosa carries the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder (~5.1 per 1000 untreated); characteristic lab and exam findings include leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis, raised BUN, metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia with purging, amenorrhea, lanugo, hypotension, hypothermia, and sinus bradycardia.

Bulimia nervosa usually occurs at normal or slightly above-normal weight, and physical exam is often unremarkable except for dental enamel erosion and parotid gland enlargement; medical danger stems from purging-related fluid/electrolyte disturbance and cardiac conduction abnormalities.

Schizophrenia requires at least two characteristic symptoms (positive and/or negative) over a 1-month period with continuous signs for at least 6 months; about 10% of patients die by suicide, and negative symptoms predominate in roughly one-third and predict poor drug response.

Personality change can be the first manifestation of serious neurologic, endocrine, or other medical disease (e.g., a frontal-lobe tumor presenting with altered motivation while the neurologic exam stays normal), so a personality disorder is a diagnosis that requires exclusion of such causes.

In somatic symptom disorder the defining feature is the patient's disproportionate interpretation and preoccupation with symptoms, not the absence of a medical explanation; patients with genuine medical disease can still qualify, and repeated tests and exploratory surgery are counterproductive.
harrison.pathophysiology: Psychiatric disorders are conceptualized as CNS disorders arising from interacting genetic, developmental, and environmental factors, with substantial heritability and considerable overlap of genetic risk variants across diagnoses (pleiotropy). Anxiety and panic involve noradrenergic discharge from the locus coeruleus and serotonergic dorsal-raphe pathways, with lactate, yohimbine, CCK-4, and CO2 capable of provoking attacks; generalized anxiety implicates the GABA-A receptor/chloride-channel complex and serotonergic modulation. PTSD is associated with excessive locus coeruleus norepinephrine release facilitating fear-memory encoding, insular threat-detection overactivity, and blunted pituitary-adrenal responses. OCD involves orbitofrontal cortex-caudate-globus pallidus circuitry. Major depression shows elevated cortisol and CRH, dexamethasone non-suppression, blunted TSH response to TRH, shortened REM latency with increased REM density and reduced slow-wave sleep, altered proinflammatory cytokines and neurotrophins, oxidative stress, telomere shortening, and possible gut-microbiome changes; delayed therapeutic action of antidepressants implicates adaptive second-messenger and neurotrophic changes. Bipolar disorder shows very high monozygotic concordance (approaching 80%) with risk genes (CACNA1C, ANK3, NCAN, ODZ4, TRANK1) shared with schizophrenia and autism, plus circadian and calcium dysregulation. Schizophrenia involves dopamine D2/D3 signaling in the ventral striatum, many small-effect GWAS loci and rare copy-number variants, and pathways of immunity, inflammation, and cell signaling.
additionalDifferentials: Major depression vs bipolar depression vs depression secondary to general medical illness or substance use
Major depressive episode vs normal bereavement/grief (grief features emptiness and wave-like pangs with preserved self-esteem)
Generalized anxiety disorder vs panic disorder (they segregate independently in families)
Schizophrenia vs schizophreniform disorder (shorter duration), schizoaffective disorder, delusional disorder, and brief psychotic disorder
Somatic symptom disorder vs illness anxiety disorder vs conversion (functional neurologic symptom) disorder vs factitious disorder vs malingering
Anorexia nervosa vs avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (the latter lacks fear of weight gain and body-image distortion)

Chronic hepatitis C-associated depression, which may worsen with interferon-alpha therapy
AIDS as a cause of secondary mania
nonInfectiousMimics: Pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, and hypoglycemia presenting as anxiety/panic
Hyperthyroidism, Huntington's disease, Wilson's disease, frontotemporal dementia, and cerebrovascular accidents presenting as secondary mania
Hypothyroidism (including subclinical) and hyperthyroidism presenting with depressed mood and cognitive/memory impairment
Frontal-lobe tumor presenting as personality change with a normal neurologic exam
Depressive pseudodementia in the elderly mimicking neurodegenerative dementia
Cardiovascular conditions (paroxysmal atrial tachycardia, mitral valve prolapse) detected on ECG/echocardiography in patients labeled with panic
Drug- or medication-induced psychosis (parkinsonian agents, clonidine, quinacrine, procaine derivatives) mimicking schizophrenia
additionalInvestigations: Targeted history, physical exam, and focused labs to exclude medical mimics of anxiety (e.g., thyroid studies, glucose, catecholamine workup as indicated)
ECG and echocardiography when a cardiovascular cause of panic-like symptoms is suspected
Thyroid function testing in mood disorders and in rapid-cycling bipolar disorder (lithium has antithyroid effects)
TCA plasma levels to guide dosing and interpret apparent treatment resistance or toxicity
Lithium blood levels (target ~0.8-1.2 meq/L acutely) given the narrow therapeutic-to-toxic window; valproate level 50-125 ug/mL; carbamazepine 4-12 ug/mL
In anorexia nervosa: CBC (leukopenia/relative lymphocytosis), electrolytes (hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis with purging), BUN, and bone-density assessment for osteoporosis
redFlags: Suicidal or homicidal ideation, a specific plan, or prior attempts - warrants immediate referral to a mental health specialist
Psychotic symptoms, mania, or severe depression/anxiety failing first-line treatment - indications for psychiatric consultation or transfer of care
Coexisting anxiety, panic, or agitation in a depressed patient, which raises near-term suicide risk
Critical weight loss, hypotension, hypothermia, bradycardia, or electrolyte/cardiac conduction abnormalities in eating disorders
Refeeding syndrome risk when restoring weight too rapidly in anorexia nervosa (target gain ~0.5-1 lb/week)
Serotonin syndrome (myoclonus, agitation, abdominal cramping, hyperpyrexia, hypertension) - a contraindication to combining MAOIs with SSRIs
Hypertensive crisis from tyramine-containing foods or sympathomimetics in patients taking MAOIs
New-onset psychosis requiring exclusion of a drug/medication cause before diagnosing schizophrenia
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely by disorder. Panic disorder responds to treatment in 75-85% of patients, though complete remission is somewhat lower. Most depressed patients (60-70%) respond to an adequately dosed antidepressant over 6-8 weeks, and about three-quarters improve by ~2 months; the best predictor of recurrence is the number of prior episodes (50-60% of first-episode patients have at least one or two recurrences). Bipolar disorder is recurrent and requires maintenance therapy; lithium responses are 70-80% in acute mania and a sustained level >=0.8 meq/L reduces suicide risk. About 4-5% of depressed and ~10% of schizophrenic patients die by suicide. Anorexia nervosa has the highest mortality of any psychiatric condition (~5.1/1000 untreated), though most patients achieve remission within 5 years; binge-eating disorder has the most favorable prognosis among eating disorders. Schizophrenia often has a poor outcome with insidious onset, but positive symptoms tend to attenuate with age and permanent remission occasionally occurs.
pitfalls: Basing psychiatric referral on the mere absence of a physical explanation rather than on positive signs/symptoms of a mental disorder
Failing to ask directly about agoraphobia, OCD behaviors, or suicidal ideation, all of which patients commonly conceal
Subjecting somatic symptom disorder patients to repeated tests and exploratory surgery, or confronting them in a way that causes humiliation and treatment abandonment
Treating an unrecognized bipolar depression with antidepressant monotherapy, risking induction of mania or cycle acceleration
Prescribing benzodiazepines beyond 4-6 weeks (tolerance, abuse, dependence) and not anticipating withdrawal, which can include seizures
Giving benzodiazepines or SSRIs in the immediate aftermath of trauma, and using debriefing, which does not prevent PTSD and may worsen symptoms
Using TCAs in patients with serious cardiovascular risk or bundle branch block, and providing large supplies to suicidal patients (TCA overdose can be lethal, desipramine highest risk)
Overlooking lithium's narrow therapeutic index and its antithyroid/renal effects during maintenance monitoring
harrison.severityClassification: Diagnoses are framed by DSM-5-TR (with ICD-10-CM used more widely worldwide); alternative research frameworks include NIMH RDoC and the dimensional HiTOP taxonomy, none yet adequately validated. Severity and subtyping markers within disorders include: bipolar I (full manic episode >=1 week) vs bipolar II (hypomania >=4 days plus recurrent depression) vs cyclothymia (>=2 years of subthreshold fluctuations); rapid cycling defined as >=4 mood episodes per year; persistent depressive (dysthymic) disorder as chronic symptoms >=2 years; PTSD specifiers (with dissociative symptoms, with delayed expression >=6 months); anorexia nervosa restricting type vs binge-eating/purging type; and Munchausen's syndrome as the most severe form of factitious disorder.
management: Use validated screening instruments such as the Patient Health Questionnaire and PC-PTSD and exclude medical mimics before confirming a primary psychiatric diagnosis
First-line pharmacotherapy for depressive and anxiety disorders with SSRIs or SNRIs, augmenting or switching for treatment resistance
Evidence-based psychotherapy, particularly cognitive behavioural therapy, alone or combined with medication
Mood stabilisers such as lithium or anticonvulsants for bipolar disorder, with therapeutic drug-level monitoring given their narrow therapeutic window and thyroid and renal surveillance on lithium
Antipsychotics for psychotic disorders and as adjuncts, with metabolic monitoring
Structured suicide risk assessment at every contact, escalating to crisis or inpatient care when risk is high
Nutritional rehabilitation with monitoring for refeeding in eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa
Manage comorbid substance misuse and coordinate care across primary care, psychiatry and psychological services
